newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW - ATT-Unisource sees huge internet sales.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - ATT-Unisource sees huge internet sales.

text.p: The AT&T-Unisource Communications venture linking the U.S. telecoms giant and the Unisource group of four major European telecoms firms sees huge revenue from its internet services by the end of 2000.
"The conservative estimate is one billion guilders ($540 million) internet sales by year-end 2000," AT&T-Unisource Communications internet access services manager Erik Neraal said on Wednesday.
The venture's internet operations notched up 1996 sales of 40 million guilders and says it is on track for sales in 1997 of around 95 million guilders.
Neraal said AT&T-Unisource was targeting big companies and major internet service providers (ISPs) in Europe, noting Unisource had offered internet services since the early 1990s.

In February 1996 Unisource had 500 corporate customers and ISPs hooked up to internet services and by the end of the year the figure for the combined AT&T-Unisource entity had risen to 1,544, he said.
"We're not going after the end-users, we're focusing solely on the business users. That's why we're so successful, because the market hasn't grown threefold in that period."

Neraal and AT&T-Unisource internet access services director Jos Gerrese said in a joint interview that the 60/40 Unisource/AT&T venture had capitalised on its European telecommunications base and expected an explosion of demand.
Business telecommunications provider Unisource is jointly owned by Koninklijke PTT Nederland, Telia of Sweden, Swiss Telecom PTT and Spain's Telefonica.

"It's a steep curve. But it's hard to target because nobody really knows what the internet market is doing. An internet year is roughly the same as a dog year, so everything doubles roughly in four months," said Gerrise.
"On a five year period you can assume safely a multiplication factor of between 2.2 and 2.5 times per year in internet business," added Neraal.

Neraal said AT&T-Unisource was aiming to be the leading provider of internet professional services in Europe, harnessing demand from corporate customers around the region, clamouring for secure, dependable internet access.
Gerrise said the partnership was attracting customers because of its size, which was set to expand dramatically with the opening up of new internet capacity in March.
"That makes us instantly the biggest internet access provider in Europe," said Gerrise, pointing out AT&T-Unisource was targeting Europe-based companies' global needs.

"It's a kind of magnet attraction, big attracts more and if you're big you can become bigger," he said, adding that AT&T-Unisource was growing faster than the market, attracting share from other players.

Neraal said the company's size and extensive network was allaying some businesses' suspicion of the internet. "Very many are afraid of connecting to the internet. They wouldn't go to a small internet provider, mainly because of security concerns."

He said corporations were coming to AT&T-Unisource with detailed requirements, wanting to set up company-wide "intranets" which give secure internet-type services within a firm and wanting to bolt on "extranets" which allow access by clearly identified parties from outside the company.
"For the past four months we've seen huge demand from corporations wanting to have a professional web-host on our network and they have very stringent requirements," he said.

"Our partners will get new subscribers and get new services on top of that. Our gut feeling is that half of the growth will come from new subscribers and the other half will come from the additional traffic generated by new services," said Neraal.
